title: Pinned Futures and Memory Stability
goal: Understand why self-referential futures require pinning before being polled.

sections.text: An async function body is compiled into a state machine enum. If that function holds references to its own local variables across an `.await`, moving the future in memory would invalidate those internal pointers.

sections.caption: Local references across await create self-referential futures.

sections.text: To prevent moving a future while polling it, Rust requires a pinned pointer, written `Pin<&mut F>`. `Pin` wraps a reference and guarantees the target will not move in memory until dropped.
Types like `Box::pin(fut)` or the `std::pin::pin!(fut)` macro pin a future so it can be safely polled or re-used in loops and macro constructs.

sections.code:
let fut = sleep(Duration::from_millis(10));
let mut pinned = std::pin::pin!(fut);
sections.caption: pin! borrows and pins a future on the stack.

sections.text: Most standard types implement `Unpin`, meaning they can move freely even when pinned. Compiler-generated futures that hold references across `.await` do NOT implement `Unpin`.

explanation: Understand why self-referential futures require pinning before being polled.
